column2: That Rama-Brahman, the empire of supreme non-duality, which is to be known through the Mahopanishad and abides as the space of consciousness, is my refuge.
Om. May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, strength and all my faculties grow strong.

All is Brahman, the Upanishad. May I never reject Brahman, and may Brahman never reject me; may there be no rejection, no rejection for me. Let the truths taught in the Upanishads abide in me, who delight in the Self; let them abide in me.
Om. Peace, peace, peace.

Now we shall explain the Mahopanishad. They say: In the beginning there was only Narayana — not Brahma, not Ishana, not the waters, not Agni and Soma, not these heaven and earth, not the stars, not the sun, not the moon. He alone found no delight. As he rested in meditation, the sacrificial hymn was uttered.

In him fourteen persons arise, and one maiden: the ten senses, the mind as the eleventh, radiance as the twelfth, egoism as the thirteenth, life-breath as the fourteenth, the Self as the fifteenth, intellect, the five elements, the five subtle elements, and the five great elements.

He is the one, the twenty-fifth Person. Having set that Person within him, no years arise for him from Prakriti; years arise afterward. Then Narayana again, desiring another, meditated with the mind. As he rested in meditation, from his forehead a three-eyed Person with a trident in his hand was born.

Bearing glory, fame, truth, celibacy, austerity, dispassion, mind, and lordship, with the sacred syllable and the utterances, the Rik, Yajus, Saman and Atharvangirasa, and all the meters, which rest on his limbs — therefore he is Ishana, Mahadeva, Mahadeva. Then Narayana again, desiring another, meditated with the mind.

As he rested in meditation, sweat fell from his forehead. Those are these spread waters. From them arose a golden orb of light. In it Brahma the four-faced was born. He meditated. Facing east: the utterance Bhuh, the Gayatri meter, the Rigveda, Agni the deity.

Facing west: the utterance Bhuvah, the Trishtubh meter, the Yajurveda, Vayu the deity. Facing north: the utterance Svah, the Jagati meter, the Samaveda, Surya the deity. Facing south: the utterance Mahah, the Anushtubh meter, the Atharvaveda, Soma the deity.

The thousand-headed god, thousand-eyed, source of the universe, supreme and eternal on all sides, the all, Narayana Hari. The Person is indeed all this, and the universe lives on him; lord of the universe, the god of universal form in the ocean. Resembling a lotus bud, it hangs like a bud.

The heart too, facing downward, for the sake of continuity. In its middle is a great flame, universal and facing every direction. In its middle a fire-flame, subtle and upright, is established. In the middle of that flame is established the Supreme Self. He is Brahma, he is Ishana, with Indra, he is the imperishable, the supreme, the self-luminous: thus the Mahopanishad.
There was one named Shuka, of great radiance, devoted to the bliss of his own nature, king of sages; from the moment of birth he attained the truth.
By his own discernment, that great-minded one himself reflected well for a long time and reached certainty of his Self.
Because it cannot be described or reached, and because the mind is the sixth sense, the Self is mere consciousness — an atom, subtler even than space.
Within the supreme atom of consciousness, crores of universes are like specks of dust; they arise, abide, and dissolve by the turning of power.
It is space because outside it is void, yet not space because it is consciousness; there is nothing that cannot be pointed to, which is called existence.
This conscious one, being luminous and having no object to know, is like a rock; yet in its own sky-like Self, established in itself, it paints the wonder of the world's unfolding.
This universe is only its radiance, so it is not apart from it; even the world's difference is its appearance, so difference too is made of it.
All-pervading, related to all, it does not go, for lack of motion; it does not exist, for lack of support — and yet it exists, being of the nature of being.
Knowledge-bliss is Brahman, the supreme refuge of the giver of gifts; it is the renunciation of all intention, which the mind clings to.
The wise say that its cognition is the absence of the waking cognitions; by its contraction and expansion the world's dissolution and creation occur.
It is the culmination of the Vedanta sayings and beyond the reach of speech: "I am Brahman, being-consciousness-supreme bliss, and nothing else."
By his own subtle intellect Shuka understood everything; having himself reached the supreme reality, his mind remained settled, unwavering.
He did not attain the belief in himself that "this is a thing." His mind simply ceased its restless attachment to objects, to many broken pleasures, as the chataka bird turns from streams of water.
Once, that one of pure insight, abiding in solitude on Meru, devoutly asked his father, the sage Krishna Dvaipayana.
O sage, how has this pageantry of the world arisen? How does it come to rest? What is it, whose is it, and when? Tell me.
Thus asked, the sage Vyasa told his son everything, as it should be told by one who knows the Self.
I have known it before, thought Shuka; and by his own understanding he did not value his father's words much.
Even the revered Vyasa, understanding his son's intention, replied again: "I do not know it truly.
There is a king named Janaka in the city of Mithila. He knows what is to be known as it is; from him you will obtain everything."
Told thus by his father, Shuka set out from Sumeru to the earth and reached the city of Videha, ruled by Janaka.
The mace-bearers informed the great Janaka: "O king, Vyasa's son Shuka stands at the door."
Saying carelessly "Let him stay there," to test Shuka, Janaka remained silent for seven days.
Then Janaka had Shuka enter the courtyard; there he stayed seven days in the same way, unmoved.
Then Janaka had him enter the inner palace court; "the king is not seen," so for seven days.
There Janaka entertained Shuka, whose face shone like the moon, with intoxicated beautiful women, with meals and heaps of pleasures.
Those pleasures and those foods did not carry away the mind of Vyasa's son, as a gentle breeze does not move a fixed mountain.
He remained only perfectly even, clear, silent, joyful in mind, spotless like the full moon, Shuka.
King Janaka, having perceived the nature of Shuka, brought him in, saw him with a joyful heart, and bowed to him.
Having completed the world's tasks and attained every desire, he welcomed him and said: "What do you wish?"
O master, how has this pageantry of the world arisen? How does it come to rest? Tell me properly and quickly.
The great Janaka told him everything exactly; that was the very thing his wise father had said earlier.

I myself had known this in particular before; when asked, my father said just this to me.
mahaupanishad:2:33	You too, best of the eloquent, have told me this same meaning; this alone is seen as the meaning of the scriptures.

Born of the mind's imagining, with the end of that imagining the burnt-out world, without essence, is destroyed.
mahaupanishad:2:35	Then is this so, O fortunate one? Tell me the unshakable truth; from you I attain rest, with a mind that wanders through the world."
Listen now to this which I tell you, O Shuka — the expanse of knowledge, the inmost essence of intellect.
By knowing which a person at once attains liberation while living.
By the knowledge that "the seen does not exist," the wiping away of the mind's seen things; when this is achieved, supreme peace of liberation arises.
The complete abandonment of impressions is the highest; the good call it liberation, the stainless way.
Those of pure impressions who do not again partake of birth and its evils, who have known what is to be known — these great-minded are called the liberated while living.
Firmness in the notion of things is called bondage; the thinning of impressions, O Brahmin, is called liberation.
He who, without any cause such as austerity, finds no delight in pleasures here — he is called liberated while living.
He who in the pleasures and pains that arrive in due time neither rejoices nor sinks — he is called liberated while living.
He who is not touched within by views of joy, anger, fear, wrath, desire or meanness — he is called liberated while living.
He who has playfully given up impressions made of egoism and remains a renouncer of objects of meditation — he is called liberated while living.
For whom, in the views within, there are no desired or undesired things, who acts as if in deep sleep — he is called liberated while living.
Delighting in the Self, seated, full, of purified mind, having reached unsurpassed rest, wishing for nothing here, living free of attachment — he is called liberated while living.
He whose unclouded awareness is not tainted even slightly in the heart-space by what is known — he is called liberated while living.
He who acts without regard to love and hatred, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, result and non-result — he is called liberated while living.
Silent, free of I-ness, free of pride, free of envy, he who acts without agitation — he is called liberated while living.
He who is free of attachment everywhere, who stays like a witness, desireless in his actions — he is called liberated while living.
He who has inwardly given up all mind-conceived merit and demerit and desire — he is called liberated while living.
He who has fully abandoned whatever whole imagining of the seen is perceived here — he is called liberated while living.
He who eats alike the bitter, sour, salty, pungent, unsweet and sweet — he is called liberated while living.
He who enjoys old age, death, calamity, kingdom and poverty alike as pleasant — he is called liberated while living.
He by whose intellect merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, death and birth are well given up — he is called liberated while living.
Free of agitation and joy, with an even, clear intellect, neither grieving nor rising — he is called liberated while living.
He by whose intellect all desires, all doubts, all strivings and all certainties have been given up — he is called liberated while living.
He whose mind is even in birth, continuance and destruction, in rising and setting — he is called liberated while living.
He who neither hates anything nor wishes for anything, who enjoys the pleasures that come naturally — he is called liberated while living.
He for whom the world's imagining is quiet, who though having parts is partless, who though having a mind is mindless — he is called liberated while living.
He who, though acting among all the webs of objects, is free of longing, full in himself as if in others' affairs — he is called liberated while living.
Having left the state of liberation-while-living when his body is given over to time, he enters the liberation without body, as wind becomes motionless.
The bodiless liberated one neither rises nor sets nor is stilled; he is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far, neither "I" nor "other."
Then there remains something, still and deep, neither light nor darkness spread, unnamed, unmanifest, merely existent.
Neither void nor form, neither seen nor sight, standing endlessly, not as a mass of elements and things.
Of an indescribable nature, fuller than full in form; neither existent nor non-existent nor both, neither being nor becoming.
Pure consciousness free of the perceived, infinite, ageless, auspicious, without beginning, middle or end, beginningless, free of disease.
That vision which is held to be in the midst of seer, seeing and seen — there is nothing higher than this, O sage, no other certainty.
You have known it yourself and heard it again from the teacher: bound by one's own intention, one is freed by non-intention.
Therefore the great soul has known by himself what is to be known; aversion to pleasures has arisen, or to all that is seen here.
You, of full mind, have obtained all that is to be obtained; in your own nature, in austerity, O Brahmin, you are free; abandon delusion.
Beyond the outer, the outer, and the inmost within the intellect, Shuka, you, seeing, do not see; you are the witness, full and alone.
Shuka rested silent in the supreme reality, in his own nature, free of grief, fear and effort, desireless, with doubts cut off.
He went to the summit of Meru for unbroken samadhi.
There, for thousands of years, in samadhi without conceptual thought, he remained in that place and became extinguished in the Self like a lamp without oil.
Purified of the stain of imagining, in the pure, spotless state of his own self, the great one, with impressions dissolved, attained oneness, like a drop of water in the ocean.
Thus the Mahopanishad.
